# Notation and Conventions {#sec-notation .unnumbered}

This section records notation used throughout the book. 

## Typography and indices

| Object | Convention | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| Scalar | italic lowercase or Greek letter | $u$, $T$, $k$, $\rho$ |
| Vector | bold lowercase letter | $\bx$, $\bu$, $\bq$ |
| Second-order tensor | bold uppercase or bold Greek letter | $\bF$, $\bC$, $\bsig$ |
| Fourth-order tensor | blackboard-bold uppercase letter | $\mathbb{C}$ |
| Set or function space | calligraphic or standard space symbol | $\Th$, $\V$, $H^1(\Om)$ |
| Matrix and coefficient vector | bold uppercase letter | $\bK$, $\bU$ |

When components are useful, Latin indices range over the spatial dimensions and
repeated indices are summed unless stated otherwise. Thus

$$
\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}=a_i b_i,
\qquad
(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{a})_i=A_{ij}a_j,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{A}:\boldsymbol{B}=A_{ij}B_{ij}.
$$


## Geometry and integration

| Symbol | Meaning | Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $d$ | Spatial dimension | $\Om\subset\R^d$ | Open physical domain |
| $\partial\Om$ | Boundary of $\Om$ | $\Gam_D$, $\Gam_N$ | Dirichlet and Neumann portions of the boundary |
| $\bx$ | Point in the spatial or current configuration | $\bX$ | Point in a reference configuration |
| $\bn$ | Outward unit normal | $\dx$, $\ds$ | Volume and boundary integration measures |

Unless a different decomposition is stated,

$$
\partial\Om=\overline{\Gam_D\cup\Gam_N},
\qquad
\Gam_D\cap\Gam_N=\varnothing.
$$


## Differential operators

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\grad u = \nabla_{\bx} u$ | Spatial gradient of a scalar field |
| $\grad\bu = \nabla_{\bx} \bu$ | Spatial gradient of a vector field |
| $\divg\bq = \nabla_{\bx}\cdot \bq$ | Spatial divergence of a vector field |
| $\divg\bsig = \nabla_{\bx}\cdot\bsig$ | Spatial divergence of a second-order tensor field |
| $\Grad\bu = \nabla_{\bX} \bu$ | Gradient with respect to reference coordinates |
| $\Div\bP = \nabla_{\bX} \cdot \bP$ | Divergence with respect to reference coordinates |

The gradient of a vector field follows the convention

$$
(\grad\bu)_{ij}=\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j},
$$

and the divergence of a second-order tensor follows

$$
(\divg\boldsymbol{A})_i
=
\frac{\partial A_{ij}}{\partial x_j}.
$$

Uppercase operators distinguish differentiation with respect to reference coordinates from differentiation with respect to spatial coordinates.

## Function spaces and variational objects

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $L^2(\Om)$ | Square-integrable scalar functions on $\Om$ |
| $L^2(\Om;\R^d)$ | Square-integrable vector fields on $\Om$ |
| $L^2(\Om;\R^{d\times d})$ | Square-integrable second-order tensor fields on $\Om$ |
| $H^m(\Om)$ | Functions with square-integrable weak derivatives through order $m$ |
| $H^m(\Om;\R^d)$ | Vector fields whose components belong to $H^m(\Om)$ |
| $H_0^1(\Om)$ | $H^1$ functions with zero prescribed boundary value |
| $V$ | Generic vector, normed, Banach, or Hilbert space |
| $\U$ | Generic trial space |
| $\V$ | Generic test or variational space |
| $\Ug$ | Trial space satisfying prescribed Dirichlet data $g$ |
| $\Vzero$ | Test space satisfying the corresponding homogeneous data |
| $a(u,v)$ | Bilinear form |
| $a(u;v)$ | Semilinear form (nonlinear in $u$ and linear in $v$) |
| $\ell(v)$ | Linear functional |
| $R(u;v)$ | Residual evaluated in direction $v$ |
| $\Pi(u)$ | Energy or potential functional |
| $\delta\Pi(u;v)$ | First variation of $\Pi$ at $u$ in direction $v$ |
| $\norm{v}_a=a(v,v)^{1/2}$ | Energy norm induced by a symmetric, coercive bilinear form |

The norm, seminorm, inner product, and duality pairing are written as

$$
\norm{v}_V,
\qquad
\seminorm{v}_{H^m(\Om)},
\qquad
\inner{u}{v}_V,
\qquad
\dual{f}{v}.
$$

## Finite element notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\Th$ | Mesh of the domain |
| $\mathcal K_e\in\Th$ | Cell $e$ in the mesh |
| $h_e$ | Diameter or characteristic size of cell $\mathcal K_e$ |
| $h=\max_{\mathcal K_e\in\Th}h_e$ | Global mesh-size parameter |
| $p$ | Polynomial degree of the finite element approximation |
| $(K,\mathcal P,\mathcal N)$ | Cell, local function space, and degrees of freedom defining a finite element |
| $\mathbb P_p$, $\mathbb Q_p$ | Polynomial spaces of degree $p$ on simplex and tensor-product cells, respectively |
| $N_c$, $N_v$, $N_n$ | Numbers of cells, mesh vertices, and finite element nodes, respectively |
| $\Uh$, $\Vh$ | Discrete trial and test spaces |
| $\uh$, $\vh$ | Discrete trial and test functions |
| $\phi_i$ | Finite element basis function |
| $I^e(a)$ | Global number of local degree of freedom $a$ on cell $e$ |
| $J^e(i)$ | Local number of global degree of freedom $i$ on cell $e$, when $i$ belongs to that cell |
| $F_e$ | Map from the reference cell $\widehat{\mathcal K}$ to $\mathcal K_e$ |
| $J_e$, $\bm J_e$ | Jacobian of $F_e$ in one and several dimensions, respectively |
| $\Ie$ | Interpolation operator on cell $\mathcal K_e$ |
| $\Ih$ | Global finite element interpolation operator |
| $\mathcal F_h$ | Set of mesh facets |
| $\mathcal Q_h$ | Local averaging or quasi-interpolation operator used in residual estimates |
| $r_e$, $j_{\mathcal F}$ | Cell and facet residuals |
| $\eta_e$ | Local a posteriori error indicator |
| $\bK\bU=\bF$ | Representative assembled algebraic system |

The book uses *cell* for a geometric member of a mesh. The calligraphic
symbols $\Ie$ and $\Ih$ denote interpolation operators. They are distinct
from the connectivity maps $I^e$ and $J^e$ and from the geometric Jacobians
$J_e$ and $\bm J_e$.

The symbols $\mathbb P_p$ and $\mathbb Q_p$ denote polynomial spaces. Phrases
such as “$P_1$ triangle,” “$P_2$ triangle,” and “$Q_1$ quadrilateral” are the
customary names of the corresponding element families.

In finite element formulas, $e$ indexes cells, $a,b$ index local degrees of
freedom, and $i,j$ index global degrees of freedom. In continuum component
notation, lowercase indices $i,j,k$ denote spatial components, while uppercase
indices $I,J,K$ denote material components when reference and current
configurations must be distinguished.

The unadorned symbol $h$ is reserved for the mesh-size parameter. For a
diffusion or heat-conduction problem, $\bq$ denotes the flux vector and

$$
q=\bq\cdot\bn
$$

denotes its outward normal component on the boundary. Thus $q>0$ represents
flux leaving the domain.

## Recurring physical fields

| Symbol | Meaning | Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $T$ | Temperature | $\bq$ | Flux vector |
| $\bu$ | Displacement vector | $\beps$ | Infinitesimal strain tensor |
| $\bsig$ | Cauchy stress tensor | $\bF$ | Deformation gradient |
| $\bC=\bF^T\bF$ | Right Cauchy--Green tensor | $\bP$ | First Piola--Kirchhoff stress tensor |
| $J = \mathrm{det}(\bF)$ | Jacobian (determinant of $\bF$) | $I_1 = \mathrm{tr}(\bC)$ | First invariant of $\bC$ (trace) |

Some standard symbols recur in different settings. In finite-deformation
mechanics, $\bF$ is the deformation gradient and $J=\det\bF$. In the assembled
finite element system, $\bF$ is the load vector. These objects do not occur in
the same derivation. Similarly, $\bm K$ is a conductivity tensor in the heat
equation and $\bK$ is a stiffness matrix in the algebraic system, while
$\bm N$ is a reference-configuration unit normal and $\bN^e$ is an element
shape-function matrix. Their meaning is stated when each setting is
introduced, and the element superscript distinguishes $\bN^e$ from the unit
normal.
